        <div class="td-content">
          
            <h1>Environments</h1>
          
          <p>Meshery Environments allow you to logically group related <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/environments/#connections">Connections</a> and their associated <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/environments/#credentials">Credentials</a>. Environments make it easier for you to manage, share, and work with a collection of resources as a group, instead of dealing with all your Connections and Credentials on an individual basis.</p>
<h3 id="assigning-resources-to-an-environment">
	Assigning Resources to an Environment
</h3>
<p>Assign any number of Connections to an environment whether that Connection is managed or unmanaged (see <a href="/v0.9/concepts/architecture/meshsync/">MeshSync</a> to learn more about managed and unmanaged Connections). In-turn, assign any number of Environments to one or more <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/workspaces/">Workspaces</a>. Connections (and any associated Credentials) that are assigned to an Environment become immediately available for use in any associated Workspace.</p>
<h3 id="sharing-resources-between-environments">
	Sharing Resources between Environments
</h3>
<p>Environments can share resources. For example, you might create an environment named &ldquo;production&rdquo; and assign three connections: a GitHub connection, a Kubernetes connection, and a Prometheus connection. Subsequently, you also define a an environment named &ldquo;dev/test &ldquo;and assign three connections: a different Kubernetes connection, a different Prometheus connection, <em>and</em> the same GitHub connection that is also assigned to the &ldquo;production&rdquo; environment.</p>
<h3 id="deleting-an-environment">
	Deleting an Environment
</h3>
<p>Deleting an environment does not delete any resources (e.g. connections) currently contained with the environment. Resources that belong to others environments will continue to belong to those other environments. Learn more about the behavior of <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/connections/">lifecycle of connections</a>.</p>
<h2 id="key-features">
	Key Features
</h2>
<ul>
<li>
<p><strong>Logical Grouping</strong> Environments allow you to logically group related connections and their associated credentials. This makes it easier to manage, share, and work with a subset of resources instead of dealing with all your connections individually.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Resource Sharing</strong> Environments can be seamlessly assigned to <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/workspaces/">Workspaces</a>, another essential concept in Meshery. When you assign an Environment to a Workspace, you enable resource sharing among team members. This collaborative approach simplifies the sharing of connections and resources, making it easier to work together in cloud-native environments.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="connections-and-credentials-as-resources">
	Connections and Credentials as Resources
</h2>
<h3 id="connections">
	Connections <a id="connections"></a>
</h3>
<p>Connections are an integral part of Environment. These are cloud-native resources that can be both managed and unmanaged, and they&rsquo;re registered by the Meshery Server. Examples of connections include Kubernetes clusters, Prometheus instances, Jaeger tracers, and Nginx web servers.</p>
<p>See &ldquo;<a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/connections/">Connections</a>&rdquo; section for more information.</p>
<h3 id="credentials">
	Credentials <a id="credentials"></a>
</h3>
<p>Credentials in an Environment are the keys to securely authenticate and access managed connections. For example, valid Prometheus secrets or Kubernetes API tokens are essential credentials for securely interacting with these managed resources.</p>
<p>See &ldquo;<a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/credentials/">Credentials</a>&rdquo; section for more information.</p>
<h2 id="environment-lifecycle">
	Environment Lifecycle
</h2>
<p>Environments in Meshery follow a defined lifecycle that helps maintain organization and control over your cloud-native resources:</p>
<h3 id="creating-environments">
	Creating Environments
</h3>
<ol>
<li>Create environments through Meshery UI or via <code>mesheryctl</code></li>
<li>Give your environment a meaningful name and description</li>
<li>Optionally add tags for better organization</li>
<li>Start assigning connections and credentials</li>
</ol>
<h3 id="managing-environments">
	Managing Environments
</h3>
<ul>
<li>Add or remove connections and credentials as needed</li>
<li>Monitor the health and status of resources within the environment</li>
<li>Configure environment-specific settings and policies</li>
<li>Share environments by assigning them to workspaces</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="environment-states">
	Environment States
</h3>
<p>Environments can exist in different states:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Active</strong>: Environment is created and ready for use</li>
<li><strong>Empty</strong>: Environment exists but has no connections assigned</li>
<li><strong>Archived</strong>: Environment is preserved but not actively used</li>
<li><strong>Deleted</strong>: Environment is removed but contained resources persist</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="best-practices">
	Best Practices
</h3>
<ul>
<li>Use clear naming conventions for environments (e.g., &ldquo;prod&rdquo;, &ldquo;staging&rdquo;, &ldquo;dev&rdquo;)</li>
<li>Document the purpose and contents of each environment</li>
<li>Regularly review and clean up unused environments</li>
<li>Implement consistent tagging across environments</li>
<li>Maintain separation between production and non-production environments</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="environment-security">
	Environment Security
</h2>
<p>Meshery implements several security measures for environments:</p>
<ul>
<li>Access control through workspace permissions</li>
<li>Credential encryption for sensitive data</li>
<li>Audit logging of environment changes</li>
<li>Resource isolation between environments</li>
</ul>
<p>By following these lifecycle and security practices, you can maintain well-organized and secure environments for your cloud-native infrastructure.</p>
<h2 id="summary">
	Summary
</h2>
<p>Environments represent a collection of resources in the form of Connections - both of managed and unmanaged Connections. Environment resources are comprised of Connections (and implicitly any Credentials used by those assigned Connections). Create and use environments to organize your connections and credentials into groups, and then make these resources available to you and your teams by assigning environments to <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/workspaces/">Workspaces</a>.</p>

        </div>

<script>
    $(document).ready(function () {

        var toc = $('#TOC');

        
        
        
        
        var hasH1 = $('.td-content h1').length > 0;
        var topSelector = hasH1 ? 'h1' : 'h2';
        var subSelector = hasH1 ? 'h2, h3' : 'h3';

        sections = $('.td-content ' + topSelector);

        $.each(sections, function (idx, v) {
            section = $(v);
            var div_id = $(section).attr('id');
            if (!section.hasClass('noTOC')) {
                var div_text = section.text().split('¶')[0];
                var parent = $("#" + div_id)
                var content = '<li id="link_' + div_id + '" class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + div_id + '" title="' + div_text + '">' + div_text + '</a></li>';
                $(document).find(toc).append(content);
            }

            
            var children = $('<nav class="md-nav"><ul class="md-nav__list"></nav></ul>')
            var contenders = $("#" + div_id).nextUntil(topSelector);
            $.each(contenders, function (idx, contender) {
                if (!$(contender).hasClass("noTOC") && $(contender).is(subSelector)) {
                    var contender_id = $(contender).attr('id');
                    var contender_text = $(contender).text().split('¶')[0];
                    var content = '<li class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + contender_id + '" title="' + contender_text + '">' + contender_text + '</a></li>';
                    children.append(content);
                }
            })
            $("#link_" + div_id).append(children);
        });
        
        $('.md-nav__link').first().addClass('selected');

        $(window).scroll(function (e) {
            
            let windowTop = $(this).scrollTop();
            
            $('.md-nav__link').each(function (event) {
                if (windowTop >= $($(this).attr('href')).offset().top - 100) {
                    
                    $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
                    
                    $(this).addClass('selected');
                }
                if ($(window).scrollTop() + $(window).height() > $(document).height() - 10) {
                    $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
                    $(this).addClass('selected');
                }
            });
        })
    });
</script>

        <div class="td-content">
          
            <h1>Logical</h1>
          
          
<p>As an extensible platform, Meshery empowers you with a wide range of logical constructs that provide support for the majority of the systems in the cloud and cloud native ecosystems. Meshery abstracts away the system specific requirements and help you focus on getting things done.</p>
<p>The logical concepts included in Meshery establish a set of foundational constructs. Each logical construct is:</p>
<ol>
<li>Versioned (see <a href="https://github.com/meshery/schemas">Schemas</a>)</li>
<li>Extensible (see <a href="/v0.9/extensibility/">Extension Points</a>)</li>
<li>Composable (see <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/patterns/">Patterns</a>)</li>
<li>Portable (see Export/Import of <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/designs/">Designs</a> and <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/models/">Models</a>)</li>
<li>Interoperable (see <a href="/v0.9/installation/compatibility-matrix/">Compatibility Matrix</a>)</li>
<li>Configurable (see <a href="/v0.9/guides/infrastructure-management/lifecycle-management/">Lifecycle Management</a>)</li>
<li>Documented (<em>you are here</em>)</li>
<li>Testable</li>
<li>Maintainable</li>
<li>Secure (v0.9.0)</li>
<li>Observable (v0.1.0)</li>
</ol>
<p>Every construct is represented in each of the following forms:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Schema</strong> (static) - the skeletal structure representing a logical view of the size, shape, characteristics of a construct.
<ul>
<li><em>Example: Component schema found in github.com/meshery/schemas</em></li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><strong>Definition</strong> (static) - An implementation of the Schema containing specific configuration for the construct at-hand.
<ul>
<li><em>Example: Component definition generically describing a Kubernetes Pod</em></li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><strong>Declaration</strong> (static) - A defined construct; A specific deof the Definition.
<ul>
<li><em>Example: Component configuration of an NGINX container as a Kubernetes Pod</em></li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><strong>Instance</strong> (dynamic) - A realized construct (deployed/discovered); An instantiation of the Declaration.
<ul>
<li><em>Example: NGINX-as234z2 pod running in cluster</em></li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="logical-concepts">
	Logical Concepts
</h2>



<ul class="section-title">

  

  
    
      <li style="list-style-type: disc; margin: 2px 0;">
        <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/components/">Components</a>

        
          - Meshery Components identify and characterize infrastructure under management.
        
      </li>
    
  
    
      <li style="list-style-type: disc; margin: 2px 0;">
        <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/connections/">Connections</a>

        
          - Meshery Connections are managed and unmanaged resources that either through discovery or manual entry are managed by a state machine and used within one or more Environments.
        
      </li>
    
  
    
      <li style="list-style-type: disc; margin: 2px 0;">
        <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/credentials/">Credentials</a>

        
          - Meshery uses one or more Credentials when authenticating to a managed or unmanaged Connection.
        
      </li>
    
  
    
      <li style="list-style-type: disc; margin: 2px 0;">
        <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/designs/">Designs</a>

        
          - Meshery Designs are descriptive, declarative characterizations of how your Kubernetes infrastructure should be configured.
        
      </li>
    
  
    
      <li style="list-style-type: disc; margin: 2px 0;">
        <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/environments/">Environments</a>

        
          - Environments are how you organize your deployment targets (whether on-premises servers or cloud services) into resource groups.
        
      </li>
    
  
    
      <li style="list-style-type: disc; margin: 2px 0;">
        <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/models/">Models</a>

        
          - Meshery uses a set of resource models to define concrete boundaries to ensure extensible and sustainable management.
        
      </li>
    
  
    
      <li style="list-style-type: disc; margin: 2px 0;">
        <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/patterns/">Patterns</a>

        
          - Meshery Patterns are descriptive, declarative characterizations of how your Kubernetes infrastructure should be configured.
        
      </li>
    
  
    
      <li style="list-style-type: disc; margin: 2px 0;">
        <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/policies/">Policies</a>

        
          - Meshery Policies enable you with a broad set of controls and governance of the behavior of systems under Meshery&#39;s management.
        
      </li>
    
  
    
      <li style="list-style-type: disc; margin: 2px 0;">
        <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/registry/">Registry</a>

        
          - Meshery Registry is a database acting as the central repository for all capabilities known to Meshery. These capabilities encompass various entities, including models, components, relationships, and policies.
        
      </li>
    
  
    
      <li style="list-style-type: disc; margin: 2px 0;">
        <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/relationships/">Relationships</a>

        
          - Meshery Relationships identify and facilitate genealogy between Components.
        
      </li>
    
  
    
      <li style="list-style-type: disc; margin: 2px 0;">
        <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/workspaces/">Workspaces</a>

        
          - Meshery Workspaces act as central collaboration point for teams.
        
      </li>
    
  

</ul>

<script>
    $(document).ready(function () {

        var toc = $('#TOC');

        
        
        
        
        var hasH1 = $('.td-content h1').length > 0;
        var topSelector = hasH1 ? 'h1' : 'h2';
        var subSelector = hasH1 ? 'h2, h3' : 'h3';

        sections = $('.td-content ' + topSelector);

        $.each(sections, function (idx, v) {
            section = $(v);
            var div_id = $(section).attr('id');
            if (!section.hasClass('noTOC')) {
                var div_text = section.text().split('¶')[0];
                var parent = $("#" + div_id)
                var content = '<li id="link_' + div_id + '" class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + div_id + '" title="' + div_text + '">' + div_text + '</a></li>';
                $(document).find(toc).append(content);
            }

            
            var children = $('<nav class="md-nav"><ul class="md-nav__list"></nav></ul>')
            var contenders = $("#" + div_id).nextUntil(topSelector);
            $.each(contenders, function (idx, contender) {
                if (!$(contender).hasClass("noTOC") && $(contender).is(subSelector)) {
                    var contender_id = $(contender).attr('id');
                    var contender_text = $(contender).text().split('¶')[0];
                    var content = '<li class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + contender_id + '" title="' + contender_text + '">' + contender_text + '</a></li>';
                    children.append(content);
                }
            })
            $("#link_" + div_id).append(children);
        });
        
        $('.md-nav__link').first().addClass('selected');

        $(window).scroll(function (e) {
            
            let windowTop = $(this).scrollTop();
            
            $('.md-nav__link').each(function (event) {
                if (windowTop >= $($(this).attr('href')).offset().top - 100) {
                    
                    $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
                    
                    $(this).addClass('selected');
                }
                if ($(window).scrollTop() + $(window).height() > $(document).height() - 10) {
                    $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
                    $(this).addClass('selected');
                }
            });
        })
    });
</script>

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8" standalone="yes"?>
<rss version="2.0" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom">
  <channel>
    <title>Logical on Documentation</title>
    <link>/v0.9/concepts/logical/</link>

    <language>en</language>
    <atom:link href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/index.xml" rel="self" type="application/rss+xml" />
    <item>
      <title>Components</title>
      <link>/v0.9/concepts/logical/components/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/concepts/logical/components/</guid>
      <description>&lt;p&gt;In Meshery, a &lt;strong&gt;Component&lt;/strong&gt; is a fundamental building block used to represent and define the infrastructure under management. Each component provides granular and specific support for your infrastructure and applications. Each component represents a distinct capability or feature, like a specific service, protocol, or configuration element. Components can be semantically meaningful (orchestratable) or non-semantically meaningful (an annotation).&lt;/p&gt;&#xA;&lt;h2 id=&#34;components-as-building-blocks&#34;&gt;&#xA;&#x9;Components as building blocks&#xA;&lt;/h2&gt;&#xA;&lt;p&gt;Meshery Models and their packaged Components represent a standardized and reusable collection of building blocks used to describe both the desired and actual configuration of infrastructure pre and post-deployment. More than this Components are using to describe non-infrastructure concepts, for example, a component might capture a comment or a visual element that you&amp;rsquo;ve placed into a Meshery Design. To aid in distinguishing between types of Components, they are categorized into two groups: Semantic and Non-Semantic components. A component is considered semantically meaningful when it behaves as a direct representation of an aspect of your infrastructure. A component is considered non-semantically meaningful when it behaves as an annotation to aid in the comprehension of your designs.&lt;/p&gt;</description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Connections</title>
      <link>/v0.9/concepts/logical/connections/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/concepts/logical/connections/</guid>
      <description>&lt;p&gt;Meshery Connections are managed and unmanaged resources that either through discovery or manual entry are tracked by Meshery. Connections can be assigned as resources to an Environment.&lt;/p&gt;&#xA;&lt;div class=&#34;alert alert-info&#34; role=&#34;alert&#34;&gt;&lt;div class=&#34;h4 alert-heading&#34; role=&#34;heading&#34;&gt;Connections as resources in Environments&lt;/div&gt;&#xA;&lt;p&gt;Meshery Environments allow you to logically group related &lt;a href=&#34;/v0.9/concepts/logical/connections/&#34;&gt;Connections&lt;/a&gt; and their associated &lt;a href=&#34;/v0.9/concepts/logical/credentials/&#34;&gt;Credentials&lt;/a&gt;. Environments make it easier for you to manage, share, and work with a collection of resources as a group, instead of dealing with all your Connections and Credentials on an individual basis.&lt;/p&gt;</description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Credentials</title>
      <link>/v0.9/concepts/logical/credentials/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/concepts/logical/credentials/</guid>
      <description>&lt;p&gt;Meshery uses one or more Credentials when authenticating to a managed or unmanaged Connection. Credentials are based on the Meshery&amp;rsquo;s &lt;a href=&#34;https://github.com/meshery/schemas/blob/master/schemas/constructs/openapi/credentials.yml&#34;&gt;Credential Schema&lt;/a&gt; with defined attributes.&lt;/p&gt;&#xA;&lt;h2 id=&#34;understanding-credentials-in-meshery&#34;&gt;&#xA;&#x9;Understanding Credentials in Meshery&#xA;&lt;/h2&gt;&#xA;&lt;p&gt;Credentials in Meshery provide secure authentication to your infrastructure and cloud native services. They are a foundational component that enables Meshery to establish and maintain secure connections with your resources.&lt;/p&gt;&#xA;&lt;h3 id=&#34;types-of-credentials&#34;&gt;&#xA;&#x9;Types of Credentials&#xA;&lt;/h3&gt;&#xA;&lt;p&gt;Meshery supports several types of credentials:&lt;/p&gt;</description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Designs</title>
      <link>/v0.9/concepts/logical/designs/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/concepts/logical/designs/</guid>
      <description>&lt;p&gt;Like a Google Doc, Designs are your primary tool for collaborative authorship of your infrastructure and services. A Design describes all the resources and their properties that you want for a single deployment based on Meshery’s declarative syntax (see &lt;a href=&#34;https://github.com/meshery/schemas&#34;&gt;Meshery Schemas repo&lt;/a&gt;). By default, Designs are stored in your user account, but can be manually exported, programmatically snapshotted, or automatically synchronized to any OCI-compatible registry (e.g. Docker Hub, AWS ECR, and so on), or Git-based repositories (coming in v0.8). You can share designs and collaborate in real-time on their creation. Designs can be imported, exported, versioned, forked, merged, snapshotted, published, shared, embedded, templatized, and more.&lt;/p&gt;</description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Environments</title>
      <link>/v0.9/concepts/logical/environments/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/concepts/logical/environments/</guid>
      <description>&lt;p&gt;Meshery Environments allow you to logically group related &lt;a href=&#34;/v0.9/concepts/logical/environments/#connections&#34;&gt;Connections&lt;/a&gt; and their associated &lt;a href=&#34;/v0.9/concepts/logical/environments/#credentials&#34;&gt;Credentials&lt;/a&gt;. Environments make it easier for you to manage, share, and work with a collection of resources as a group, instead of dealing with all your Connections and Credentials on an individual basis.&lt;/p&gt;&#xA;&lt;h3 id=&#34;assigning-resources-to-an-environment&#34;&gt;&#xA;&#x9;Assigning Resources to an Environment&#xA;&lt;/h3&gt;&#xA;&lt;p&gt;Assign any number of Connections to an environment whether that Connection is managed or unmanaged (see &lt;a href=&#34;/v0.9/concepts/architecture/meshsync/&#34;&gt;MeshSync&lt;/a&gt; to learn more about managed and unmanaged Connections). In-turn, assign any number of Environments to one or more &lt;a href=&#34;/v0.9/concepts/logical/workspaces/&#34;&gt;Workspaces&lt;/a&gt;. Connections (and any associated Credentials) that are assigned to an Environment become immediately available for use in any associated Workspace.&lt;/p&gt;</description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Models</title>
      <link>/v0.9/concepts/logical/models/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/concepts/logical/models/</guid>
      <description>&lt;p&gt;Models are units of packaging for definitions of Meshery&amp;rsquo;s logical object representations. Each model is versioned and encompasses a collection of components, relationships, policies, connections, and credentials. Meshery&amp;rsquo;s internal object model provides a consistent and extensible way of capturing and characterizing the resources (applications, services, and infrastructure) under Meshery&amp;rsquo;s management. Each model is versioned and bundles definitions of any number of components, relationships, policies, connections and credentials. Additionally, models can be exported as OCI-compatible images, defining the managed infrastructure, their interrelationships, and specific management details.&lt;/p&gt;</description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Patterns</title>
      <link>/v0.9/concepts/logical/patterns/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/concepts/logical/patterns/</guid>
      <description>&lt;p&gt;A Pattern is a templated design. Patterns promote reuse. Patterns are higher level abstractions of designs, in which a complex design is represented as a single component, promoting consistent infrastructure management practices as it hides the complexity of it&amp;rsquo;s underlying design. Patterns enable you to establish best practices and propagate the use of these practices in a simple consumable single component. Once created, a pattern becomes available for use alongside other components.&lt;/p&gt;</description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Policies</title>
      <link>/v0.9/concepts/logical/policies/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/concepts/logical/policies/</guid>
      <description>&lt;p&gt;Policies offer an evaluation algorithm to ensure desired behavior enforcement. Policies can be applied to components and relationships, defining rules and actions based on predefined conditions.&lt;/p&gt;&#xA;&lt;h2 id=&#34;policy-evaluation&#34;&gt;&#xA;&#x9;Policy Evaluation&#xA;&lt;/h2&gt;&#xA;&lt;p&gt;The relationships are a powerful way to design your infrastructure and each of them are backed by one or more policies. Policies evaluate the designs for potential relationships and the decide whether to create/delete/update the relationships.&lt;/p&gt;&#xA;&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href=&#34;/v0.9/concepts/logical/policies/images/meshery-models-policy-evaluation.svg&#34;&gt;&lt;img class=&#34;content-image&#34; src=&#34;./images/meshery-models-policy-evaluation.svg&#34; alt=&#34;Meshery Models Policy Evaluation&#34;  /&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Registry</title>
      <link>/v0.9/concepts/logical/registry/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/concepts/logical/registry/</guid>
      <description>&lt;h1 id=&#34;meshery-registry-a-central-hub-for-capabilities&#34;&gt;&#xA;&#x9;Meshery Registry: A Central Hub for Capabilities&#xA;&lt;/h1&gt;&#xA;&lt;p&gt;The Meshery Registry is a vital component within Meshery, serving as a centralized repository for managing a diverse range of cloud and cloud native resources. It stores and organizes crucial information such as models, categories, components, and relationships, enabling efficient interaction and utilization of these resources within the Meshery ecosystem. You can conveniently &lt;a href=&#34;/v0.9/concepts/logical/registry/#interacting-with-the-meshery-registry&#34;&gt;access and manage registry data&lt;/a&gt; through Meshery UI, and through Meshery CLI (&lt;a href=&#34;/v0.9/reference/mesheryctl/registry/&#34;&gt;mesheryctl registry&lt;/a&gt;).&lt;/p&gt;</description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Relationships</title>
      <link>/v0.9/concepts/logical/relationships/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/concepts/logical/relationships/</guid>
      <description>&lt;p&gt;Meshery Relationships characterize how &lt;a href=&#34;/v0.9/concepts/logical/components/&#34;&gt;components&lt;/a&gt; are connected and interact with each other. Relationships are defined within &lt;a href=&#34;/v0.9/concepts/logical/models/&#34;&gt;models&lt;/a&gt; to aid in structuring the interrelationships between one or more components in a &lt;a href=&#34;/v0.9/concepts/logical/designs/&#34;&gt;design&lt;/a&gt; to further in comprehending the overall structure and dependencies within managed systems.&lt;/p&gt;&#xA;&lt;p&gt;Meshery recognizes that relationships exist in various forms and that the existence of a relationship might be interdependent upon the existence (or absence) of another relationship. To support this complexity, Meshery relationships are highly expressive, characterizing the nature of interaction of interconnected components no matter their genealogy.&lt;/p&gt;</description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Workspaces</title>
      <link>/v0.9/concepts/logical/workspaces/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/concepts/logical/workspaces/</guid>
      <description>&lt;p&gt;Like a Google Drive, Meshery Workspaces serve as a virtual space for your team-based work. Create a Workspace to organize your work and to serve as the central point of collaboration for you and your teams and a central point of access control to Environments and their resources.&lt;/p&gt;&#xA;&lt;p&gt;You may create Workspaces to organize project-based work or to create domains of responsibility for your teams or segregate Designs and Environments and track team activity.&lt;/p&gt;</description>
    </item>
  </channel>
</rss>

        <div class="td-content">
          
            <h1>Models</h1>
          
          <p>Models are units of packaging for definitions of Meshery&rsquo;s logical object representations. Each model is versioned and encompasses a collection of components, relationships, policies, connections, and credentials. Meshery&rsquo;s internal object model provides a consistent and extensible way of capturing and characterizing the resources (applications, services, and infrastructure) under Meshery&rsquo;s management. Each model is versioned and bundles definitions of any number of components, relationships, policies, connections and credentials. Additionally, models can be exported as OCI-compatible images, defining the managed infrastructure, their interrelationships, and specific management details.</p>
<h2 id="key-aspects-of-meshery-models">
	Key aspects of Meshery Models
</h2>
<p>Models serve as the foundational packaging units for Meshery&rsquo;s logical object representations. Each model is versioned and encompasses a collection of components, relationships, policies, connections, and credentials. Designed for consistency and extensibility, Meshery&rsquo;s internal object model effectively captures and characterizes the resources—such as applications, services, and infrastructure—under its management. Additionally, models can be exported as OCI-compatible images, defining the managed infrastructure, their interrelationships, and specific management details.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Logical Representation:</strong> Models offer a logical representation of entities under Meshery&rsquo;s management, abstracting away system-specific details.</li>
<li><strong>Packaging:</strong> Model packages can be imported and exported as OCI-compatible images, ensuring portability and encapsulation of intellectual property.</li>
<li><strong>Components:</strong> Components within a Model represent the capabilities of the underlying platform and are used by operators to build applications.</li>
<li><strong>Relationships:</strong> Relationships define interactions and dependencies between components within a model.</li>
<li><strong>Policies:</strong> Policies govern the behavior and constraints of components and relationships, ensuring adherence to desired operational practices.</li>
<li><strong>Extensibility:</strong> Models are highly extensible, allowing you to define custom components, relationships, and policies.</li>
</ul>
<div class="alert alert-light" role="alert"><div class="h4 alert-heading" role="heading">Creating your own models</div>
<p>If you would like to create your own, augment existing models, or contribute new models, please refer to the <a href="/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-models/">Contributing to Models</a> guide.</p>
</div>
<p>See <a href="/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-models/">Contributing to Models</a>.</p>
<p>As a cloud native manager that provides a comprehensive set of tools for managing multi-cloud and cloud native applications and infrastructure, Meshery needs object models that can granularly characterize a wide range of systems under management from simple applications to complex microservices architectures and their infrastructure. This document describes the Meshery Model and its constituent set of entities  used to represent and manage cloud and cloud native systems.</p>
<p>Using Meshery Models, users can define and manage cloud-native systems, including applications, services, and infrastructure. Models provide a way to represent the desired state of the system, and they can be used to deploy, monitor, and manage cloud-native applications. Models are designed to be extensible, allowing users to define new constructs as needed. They are also machine-readable, allowing them to be used by automation tools.</p>
<h3 id="model-portability-and-your-intellectual-property">
	Model Portability and Your Intellectual Property
</h3>
<p>Each model (package) can be imported and exported from Meshery Server as OCI-compatible images. This makes models portable, abstracts their complexity, and encapsulates intellectual property that you might have created while designing your own models. Model packages are versioned and bundle any number of components, relationships, policies, connections, and credentials.</p>
<p>Models are stored in Meshery&rsquo;s <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/registry/">registry</a> where they can be:</p>
<ul>
<li>Discovered and reused by teams</li>
<li>Versioned and tagged</li>
<li>Shared publicly or kept private</li>
<li>Extended and customized</li>
</ul>
<p>The registry provides a central location for managing and distributing your infrastructure models.</p>
<p>Every entity type is implemented by a <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/registry/">registrant</a>. Without registrants and models, Meshery can&rsquo;t manage any kind of infrastructure.</p>
<p>Most registrants configure a specific infrastructure platform (either cloud or self-hosted). Registrants vary in their capabilities. Capabilities come in the form of components, some of which represent infrastructure to be managed others of which represent functional additional functionality to augment Meshery&rsquo;s behavior and deepen its feature set. Some registrants offer infrastructure-specific orchestration. For example the Meshery Adapter for Istio offers integration with each of Istio&rsquo;s addons. Others registrants offer specific services. For example, the Meshery Adapter for Nighthawk offers load generation and service performance characteriazation.</p>
<h2 id="design-principles">
	Design Principles
</h2>
<p>Meshery Models adhere to several design principles, including establishing a set of constructs, clearly defining construct boundaries, allowing construct extension, reusing existing models, being user-centric, and simplifying complex networking and distributed systems. Meshery Models is designed to meet the following goals:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Comprehensive:</strong> The model should be able to represent a wide range of cloud and cloud native resources.</li>
<li><strong>Extensible:</strong> The model should be extensible, allowing new constructs to be added as needed.</li>
<li><strong>User-centric:</strong> The model should be easy for users to understand and use.</li>
<li><strong>Machine-readable:</strong> The model should be machine-readable, allowing it to be used by automation tools.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="models-as-the-unit-of-packaging">
	Models as the Unit of Packaging
</h2>
<p>Each model package can be imported and exported from the system as OCI-compatible images, making them portable (a design goal), abstracting their complexity, and encapsulating potential intellectual property that users might have invested into their models. Model packages are versioned and bundle any number of components, relationships, policies, connections and credentials. For example:</p>
<div class="alert alert-info" role="alert"><div class="h4 alert-heading" role="heading">Model Packaging</div>
<p>Model constructs can be packaged and exported as OCI-compatible images. This makes them portable and allows them to be shared between different environments.</p>
</div>
<p><img class="content-image" src="./images/meshery-models.png" alt="Meshery Models"  />
<em>Figure: Model Construct Classification</em></p>
<h2 id="key-aspects-and-characteristics">
	Key aspects and characteristics
</h2>
<p>You might not fully comprehend the Meshery Models figure above. The following analogy offers an alternative viewpoint from which to comprehend the Capabilities Registry (where Models are imported and their capabilities registered for use).</p>
<p><img class="content-image" src="./images/meshery-models-analogy.svg" alt="Meshery Models Analogy"  />
<em>Figure: Registrar&rsquo;s Office and Meshery Models Analogy</em></p>
<h3 id="models">
	Models
</h3>
<p>Models introduce various core constructs that form the foundation of the model. Some of the core constructs mentioned in the document include Components, Designs, Policies, and Relationships. Models having the same <code>name</code> and <code>version</code> attributes are considered duplicates.</p>
<h3 id="component">
	Component
</h3>
<p><a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/components/">Component</a> represent entities in the Meshery ecosystem, exposing capabilities of the underlying platform. They can be registered, created, and used by users and operators. Components have definitions, instances, and associated metadata. Components having the same <code>kind</code>, <code>apiVersion</code> and <code>model.name</code> attributes are considered duplicates.</p>
<h3 id="policy">
	Policy
</h3>
<p><a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/policies/">Policies</a> includes constructs for managing metrics, defining actions, and specifying color properties of components or designs. These constructs help in monitoring, controlling, and visualizing different aspects of the Meshery ecosystem.</p>
<h3 id="relationships">
	Relationships
</h3>
<p><a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/relationships/">Relationships</a> define the nature of interaction between interconnected components in Model. They represent various types of connections and dependencies between components, such as hierarchical, network, or default relationships. Relationships have selectors, metadata, and optional parameters.</p>
<h4 id="evaluation-of-relationships">
	Evaluation of Relationships
</h4>
<p>Meshery provides a relationship evaluation algorithm to ensure desired behavior enforcement. <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/policies/">Policies</a> can be applied to components and relationships, defining rules and actions based on predefined conditions.</p>
<div class="alert alert-info" role="alert"><div class="h4 alert-heading" role="heading">Model Schema</div>
<p>Model constructs are defined using a schema language called Cue. Cue is a powerful and expressive language that is well-suited for defining cloud-native constructs.</p>
</div>
<h3 id="designs">
	Designs
</h3>
<p><a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/designs/">Designs</a> are deployable units in Meshery that describe the desired infrastructure. They consist of components and patterns, allowing users to define and configure the behavior of their cloud-native applications. A design is a collection of components and patterns that represent a desired state of infrastructure. Designs are used to deploy and manage cloud-native systems.</p>
<h3 id="patterns">
	Patterns
</h3>
<p><a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/patterns/">Patterns</a> are reusable configuration that can be applied to components or designs. They define best practices for configuring and operating cloud-native application functionality. Patterns can be applied to components or designs, and they are read-only.</p>
<div class="alert alert-info" role="alert"><div class="h4 alert-heading" role="heading">Metadata</div>
<p>Metadata provide additional details about a component in Meshery. They offer specific functionality or characteristics associated with a component, enhancing its capabilities. Metadata can be attached to components to customize their behavior.</p>
</div>
<h2 id="versioning">
	Versioning
</h2>
<p><img class="content-image" src="./images/versioning-meshery-entities.svg" alt="Versioning Models"  /></p>
<h2 id="summary">
	Summary
</h2>
<p>A Model serves as a unit of packaging for Meshery&rsquo;s logical object representation. Models encompass a structured framework that defines the components, relationships, policies, and other elements that constitute a system or application under Meshery&rsquo;s management. Models offer a way to encapsulate the complexities of diverse systems and provide a standardized representation for management and interaction.</p>
<p>Models are a powerful way to define, package and share your infrastructure configurations in Meshery. They provide a consistent, portable format for managing cloud native systems while enabling reuse and collaboration across teams.</p>
<p>By using models, you can:</p>
<ul>
<li>Define infrastructure in a standardized way</li>
<li>Package related resources together</li>
<li>Share and reuse configurations</li>
<li>Track changes through versioning</li>
<li>Extend and customize for your needs</li>
</ul>

        </div>

<script>
    $(document).ready(function () {

        var toc = $('#TOC');

        
        
        
        
        var hasH1 = $('.td-content h1').length > 0;
        var topSelector = hasH1 ? 'h1' : 'h2';
        var subSelector = hasH1 ? 'h2, h3' : 'h3';

        sections = $('.td-content ' + topSelector);

        $.each(sections, function (idx, v) {
            section = $(v);
            var div_id = $(section).attr('id');
            if (!section.hasClass('noTOC')) {
                var div_text = section.text().split('¶')[0];
                var parent = $("#" + div_id)
                var content = '<li id="link_' + div_id + '" class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + div_id + '" title="' + div_text + '">' + div_text + '</a></li>';
                $(document).find(toc).append(content);
            }

            
            var children = $('<nav class="md-nav"><ul class="md-nav__list"></nav></ul>')
            var contenders = $("#" + div_id).nextUntil(topSelector);
            $.each(contenders, function (idx, contender) {
                if (!$(contender).hasClass("noTOC") && $(contender).is(subSelector)) {
                    var contender_id = $(contender).attr('id');
                    var contender_text = $(contender).text().split('¶')[0];
                    var content = '<li class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + contender_id + '" title="' + contender_text + '">' + contender_text + '</a></li>';
                    children.append(content);
                }
            })
            $("#link_" + div_id).append(children);
        });
        
        $('.md-nav__link').first().addClass('selected');

        $(window).scroll(function (e) {
            
            let windowTop = $(this).scrollTop();
            
            $('.md-nav__link').each(function (event) {
                if (windowTop >= $($(this).attr('href')).offset().top - 100) {
                    
                    $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
                    
                    $(this).addClass('selected');
                }
                if ($(window).scrollTop() + $(window).height() > $(document).height() - 10) {
                    $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
                    $(this).addClass('selected');
                }
            });
        })
    });
</script>

        <div class="td-content">
          
            <h1>Patterns</h1>
          
          <p>A Pattern is a templated design. Patterns promote reuse. Patterns are higher level abstractions of designs, in which a complex design is represented as a single component, promoting consistent infrastructure management practices as it hides the complexity of it&rsquo;s underlying design. Patterns enable you to establish best practices and propagate the use of these practices in a simple consumable single component. Once created, a pattern becomes available for use alongside other components.</p>
<div class="alert alert-warning" role="alert"><div class="h4 alert-heading" role="heading">Future Feature</div>
<p>Patterns are a roadmap item, planned for v0.9.0.</p>
</div>

<script>
    $(document).ready(function () {

        var toc = $('#TOC');

        
        
        
        
        var hasH1 = $('.td-content h1').length > 0;
        var topSelector = hasH1 ? 'h1' : 'h2';
        var subSelector = hasH1 ? 'h2, h3' : 'h3';

        sections = $('.td-content ' + topSelector);

        $.each(sections, function (idx, v) {
            section = $(v);
            var div_id = $(section).attr('id');
            if (!section.hasClass('noTOC')) {
                var div_text = section.text().split('¶')[0];
                var parent = $("#" + div_id)
                var content = '<li id="link_' + div_id + '" class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + div_id + '" title="' + div_text + '">' + div_text + '</a></li>';
                $(document).find(toc).append(content);
            }

            
            var children = $('<nav class="md-nav"><ul class="md-nav__list"></nav></ul>')
            var contenders = $("#" + div_id).nextUntil(topSelector);
            $.each(contenders, function (idx, contender) {
                if (!$(contender).hasClass("noTOC") && $(contender).is(subSelector)) {
                    var contender_id = $(contender).attr('id');
                    var contender_text = $(contender).text().split('¶')[0];
                    var content = '<li class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + contender_id + '" title="' + contender_text + '">' + contender_text + '</a></li>';
                    children.append(content);
                }
            })
            $("#link_" + div_id).append(children);
        });
        
        $('.md-nav__link').first().addClass('selected');

        $(window).scroll(function (e) {
            
            let windowTop = $(this).scrollTop();
            
            $('.md-nav__link').each(function (event) {
                if (windowTop >= $($(this).attr('href')).offset().top - 100) {
                    
                    $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
                    
                    $(this).addClass('selected');
                }
                if ($(window).scrollTop() + $(window).height() > $(document).height() - 10) {
                    $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
                    $(this).addClass('selected');
                }
            });
        })
    });
</script>

        <div class="td-content">
          
            <h1>Policies</h1>
          
          <p>Policies offer an evaluation algorithm to ensure desired behavior enforcement. Policies can be applied to components and relationships, defining rules and actions based on predefined conditions.</p>
<h2 id="policy-evaluation">
	Policy Evaluation
</h2>
<p>The relationships are a powerful way to design your infrastructure and each of them are backed by one or more policies. Policies evaluate the designs for potential relationships and the decide whether to create/delete/update the relationships.</p>
<p><a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/policies/images/meshery-models-policy-evaluation.svg"><img class="content-image" src="./images/meshery-models-policy-evaluation.svg" alt="Meshery Models Policy Evaluation"  /></a></p>
<p>Meshery Server has a built-in policy engine, based on Open Policy Agent (OPA). Currently, Meshery Server is the only place where the policy evals occur. Policy evaluation is invoked each time a design is updated, and each time a design is imported. By default, policies evaluate for all registered relationships.</p>
<p>In any given Meshery deployment, you can reference and search the full set of registered policies (in Meshery&rsquo;s internal registry) in using either of Meshery&rsquo;s client interfaces.</p>
<div class="alert alert-info" role="alert"><div class="h4 alert-heading" role="heading">Viewing All Registered Relationships</div>
<p>You can view all registered relationships using either Meshery UI or Meshery CLI.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Using Meshery UI</strong>: Navigate to <em>Settings</em>, then to <em>Registry</em></li>
<li><strong>Using Meshery CLI</strong>: <code>mesheryctl policy list</code></li>
</ul>
</div>
<!-- There are different points in time in which policy evaluations are invoked

1. Each time the design is updated.
2. A Design/HelmChart/K8s Manifest/Docker Compose app is imported/uploaded.
3. Ad-hoc invocation from the Actions Center (coming soon).  -->
<h3 id="how-are-conflicts-resolved">
	How are conflicts resolved?
</h3>
<p>In the event of a conflict or tie, Meshery relies on Open Policy Agent&rsquo;s <a href="https://www.openpolicyagent.org/docs/latest/faq/">reconciliation behavior</a> for conflict resolution.</p>
<div class="alert alert-warning" role="alert"><div class="h4 alert-heading" role="heading">Conflict Resolution</div>
<p>It may happen that certain eval decisions contain results such that two different components create a conflicting relationship with same component. While this is semantically correct, the visual representation of the relationship in such cases may be undesirable, and you may see relationships and components being redrawn depending upon how the client / Meshery UI visualizes the relationships.</p>
</div>
<p>For an in-depth review, watch this meeting recording.</p>
<iframe width="560" height="315" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/XrLpBVsm6nk?si=j-igwtd_gQ0N61vV&amp;start=453" title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>
<div class="alert alert-dark" role="alert"><div class="h4 alert-heading" role="heading">Future Feature</div>
<p>Policy evaluation in WASM runtime is on roadmap for Meshery v0.8.3.</p>
</div>

        </div>

<script src="https://code.jquery.com/jquery-3.3.1.min.js"

<script>
    $(document).ready(function () {

        var toc = $('#TOC');

        
        
        
        
        var hasH1 = $('.td-content h1').length > 0;
        var topSelector = hasH1 ? 'h1' : 'h2';
        var subSelector = hasH1 ? 'h2, h3' : 'h3';

        sections = $('.td-content ' + topSelector);

        $.each(sections, function (idx, v) {
            section = $(v);
            var div_id = $(section).attr('id');
            if (!section.hasClass('noTOC')) {
                var div_text = section.text().split('¶')[0];
                var parent = $("#" + div_id)
                var content = '<li id="link_' + div_id + '" class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + div_id + '" title="' + div_text + '">' + div_text + '</a></li>';
                $(document).find(toc).append(content);
            }

            
            var children = $('<nav class="md-nav"><ul class="md-nav__list"></nav></ul>')
            var contenders = $("#" + div_id).nextUntil(topSelector);
            $.each(contenders, function (idx, contender) {
                if (!$(contender).hasClass("noTOC") && $(contender).is(subSelector)) {
                    var contender_id = $(contender).attr('id');
                    var contender_text = $(contender).text().split('¶')[0];
                    var content = '<li class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + contender_id + '" title="' + contender_text + '">' + contender_text + '</a></li>';
                    children.append(content);
                }
            })
            $("#link_" + div_id).append(children);
        });
        
        $('.md-nav__link').first().addClass('selected');

        $(window).scroll(function (e) {
            
            let windowTop = $(this).scrollTop();
            
            $('.md-nav__link').each(function (event) {
                if (windowTop >= $($(this).attr('href')).offset().top - 100) {
                    
                    $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
                    
                    $(this).addClass('selected');
                }
                if ($(window).scrollTop() + $(window).height() > $(document).height() - 10) {
                    $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
                    $(this).addClass('selected');
                }
            });
        })
    });
</script>

          <h1 id="meshery-registry-a-central-hub-for-capabilities">
	Meshery Registry: A Central Hub for Capabilities
</h1>
<p>The Meshery Registry is a vital component within Meshery, serving as a centralized repository for managing a diverse range of cloud and cloud native resources. It stores and organizes crucial information such as models, categories, components, and relationships, enabling efficient interaction and utilization of these resources within the Meshery ecosystem. You can conveniently <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/registry/#interacting-with-the-meshery-registry">access and manage registry data</a> through Meshery UI, and through Meshery CLI (<a href="/v0.9/reference/mesheryctl/registry/">mesheryctl registry</a>).</p>
<p>As the central repository for all capabilities known to Meshery, the registry contains various entities.</p>
<details>
  <summary>Contents of the Registry</summary>
  <br /><br />
  <a href="../models">Models</a>: Blueprints defining configurations for interacting with cloud native infrastructure. They consist of operations, components, relationships, and policies.
  <ul>
    <li><a href="../components">Components</a>: Reusable building blocks for depicting capabilities defined within models.</li>
    <li><a href="../relationships">Relationships</a>: Define the nature of connections between components within a model, describing how they interact and depend on each other.</li>
    <li><a href="../policies">Policies</a>: Enforce specific rules and governance for system behavior under Meshery's management.</li>
    <li><a href="../connections">Connections</a>: Managed and unmanaged resources that Meshery can interact with.</li>
    <li><a href="../credentials">Credentials</a>: Optionally, included secrets associated with connections contained in a model.</li>
  </ul>
  <br />
</details>
<h2 id="key-concepts-and-terminology">
	Key Concepts and Terminology
</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>Registry</strong>: a component within Meshery that contains a database of known capabilities.</li>
<li><strong>Registrar</strong>: The internal Meshery Server process responsible for managing and maintaining the registry.</li>
<li><strong>Registrant</strong> (Entity Source): The source of an entity (e.g., model file, Kubernetes cluster).
Entity (Registree): An individual capability stored in the registry (e.g., model, component).</li>
<li><strong>Registrant</strong> <em>(Host)</em>: A Meshery Connection responsible for sourcing and registering entities. A registrant can perform registration for their own entities, or a registrant can act as a proxy on behalf of a third-party entity source.</li>
<li><strong>Entity</strong> <em>(registree)</em> - an entry in the Meshery Registry; e.g. a model, component, relationship, or policy. Sometimes referred to as a capability.</li>
</ul>
<!-- - **Entity Source**: an entity’s original location from which it was sourced; e.g. (source_uri is used as the flag by Meshery Server to assess whether additional support). The Entity Source should have all the information that Meshery needs to generate the components.   -->
<h2 id="models-in-the-registry">
	Models in the Registry
</h2>
<p>You will find two types of models in the registry: Static and Dynamic.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Static Models:</strong> Pre-defined models included with each Meshery release. See the full list of static models.</li>
<li><strong>Dynamic Models:</strong> Generated at run-time by connecting Meshery to supported platforms like Kubernetes clusters or cloud providers.</li>
</ul>
<p>Each Meshery release comes with a built-in set of models automatically registered at Meshery Server boot-time. These built-in models offer a core set of entities for Meshery&rsquo;s supported <a href="/extensibility/integrations">integrations</a>. Once Meshery Server is running, and as it connects to and discovers your infrastructure, <em>dynamic models</em> are automatically generated. A given Meshery release may not include all possible models found in your environment, so Meshery automatically generates <em>and registers</em> new models and components based on the specific infrastructure Meshery is connected to. Dyanmic models often lack additional metadata, such as descriptions, tags, and relationships, which are typically included in static models.</p>
<h2 id="interacting-with-the-meshery-registry">
	Interacting with the Meshery Registry
</h2>
<p>Use either Meshery UI or CLI to interact with the Registry. Meshery UI offers a user-friendly visual interface for browsing, searching, and managing registry entries. You can easily explore available models, components, and relationships, gaining insights into their properties and connections. Meshery CLI offers commands so that you can register, list, retrieve, update, and delete models, components, and relationships directly from the command line.</p>
<h3 id="model-generation">
	Model Generation
</h3>
<p>The process of generating a Model (and its entities) is a multi-step process and does not require use of Meshery Server. The process begins with the sourcing of the model information from an authoritative source: a Registrant. Registrants are responsible for providing all the necessary information to Meshery to generate the model.</p>
<h4 id="using-meshery-cli-to-generate-models">
	Using Meshery CLI to Generate Models
</h4>
<p>Meshery CLI supports the generation of models from a Google Spreadsheet. The Google Spreadsheet should contain a list of model names and source locations from any supported Registrant (e.g. GitHub, Artifact Hub) repositories. The source locations can be a URL to a folder containing Kubernetes CRDs, or to a Helm Chart tar.gz, or an individual Kubernetes Manifest with custom resource definition.</p>
<p>See <a href="/v0.9/reference/mesheryctl/registry/generate/"><code>mesheryctl registry generate</code></a> for more information.</p>
<h3 id="model-registration">
	Model Registration
</h3>
<p>Once registered in the Meshery Registry, Models and their entities are available for use within that specific Meshery Server.</p>
<p>Meshery <a href="/v0.9/concepts/architecture/adapters/">Adapters</a> are one example of a Registrant. Registrants are responsible for the registration of entities in the Meshery Registry. Adapters are responsible for the sourcing and registration of entities and the packaging of these enties into one or more models.</p>
<h4 id="using-meshery-cli-to-register-a-model">
	Using Meshery CLI to Register a Model
</h4>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">mesheryctl model import -f &lt;path-to-model&gt;
</span></span></code></pre></div><h4 id="using-meshery-ui-to-register-a-model">
	Using Meshery UI to Register a Model
</h4>
<p>Visit the Settings Registry page and click the &ldquo;Import&rdquo; button to import a model.</p>
<h3 id="ignoring-an-entity">
	Ignoring an Entity
</h3>
<p>You have control over whether a registered entity (model and all that the model contains) this can be an individual or team-level preference. Use the &ldquo;Ignore&rdquo; action to designate whether a given model is allowed to be used within a given Meshery Server deployment. Models that are ignored remain in the Meshery Registry but are not available for use within a given Meshery Server deployment.</p>

        </div>

<script>
    $(document).ready(function () {

        var toc = $('#TOC');

        
        
        
        
        var hasH1 = $('.td-content h1').length > 0;
        var topSelector = hasH1 ? 'h1' : 'h2';
        var subSelector = hasH1 ? 'h2, h3' : 'h3';

        sections = $('.td-content ' + topSelector);

        $.each(sections, function (idx, v) {
            section = $(v);
            var div_id = $(section).attr('id');
            if (!section.hasClass('noTOC')) {
                var div_text = section.text().split('¶')[0];
                var parent = $("#" + div_id)
                var content = '<li id="link_' + div_id + '" class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + div_id + '" title="' + div_text + '">' + div_text + '</a></li>';
                $(document).find(toc).append(content);
            }

            
            var children = $('<nav class="md-nav"><ul class="md-nav__list"></nav></ul>')
            var contenders = $("#" + div_id).nextUntil(topSelector);
            $.each(contenders, function (idx, contender) {
                if (!$(contender).hasClass("noTOC") && $(contender).is(subSelector)) {
                    var contender_id = $(contender).attr('id');
                    var contender_text = $(contender).text().split('¶')[0];
                    var content = '<li class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + contender_id + '" title="' + contender_text + '">' + contender_text + '</a></li>';
                    children.append(content);
                }
            })
            $("#link_" + div_id).append(children);
        });
        
        $('.md-nav__link').first().addClass('selected');

        $(window).scroll(function (e) {
            
            let windowTop = $(this).scrollTop();
            
            $('.md-nav__link').each(function (event) {
                if (windowTop >= $($(this).attr('href')).offset().top - 100) {
                    
                    $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
                    
                    $(this).addClass('selected');
                }
                if ($(window).scrollTop() + $(window).height() > $(document).height() - 10) {
                    $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
                    $(this).addClass('selected');
                }
            });
        })
    });
</script>

        <div class="td-content">
          
            <h1>Relationships</h1>
          
          <p>Meshery Relationships characterize how <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/components/">components</a> are connected and interact with each other. Relationships are defined within <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/models/">models</a> to aid in structuring the interrelationships between one or more components in a <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/designs/">design</a> to further in comprehending the overall structure and dependencies within managed systems.</p>
<p>Meshery recognizes that relationships exist in various forms and that the existence of a relationship might be interdependent upon the existence (or absence) of another relationship. To support this complexity, Meshery relationships are highly expressive, characterizing the nature of interaction of interconnected components no matter their genealogy.</p>
<p><strong>Benefits of Using Meshery Relationships</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Improved Visibility:</strong> Relationships provide a clear visual representation of the connections between components, making it easier to understand the system&rsquo;s architecture.</li>
<li><strong>Enhanced Design:</strong> Relationships help you make informed decisions about component selection and placement, leading to better design choices.</li>
<li><strong>Automated Configuration:</strong> Relationship-driven actions can automate the configuration of components, reducing manual effort and potential errors.</li>
<li><strong>Increased Flexibility:</strong> The use of selectors, actions, and operators provides flexibility in defining and managing relationships.</li>
</ul>
<div class="alert alert-dark" role="alert"><div class="h4 alert-heading" role="heading">Contributor Guide to Meshery Relationships</div>
<p>If you want to create a new relationship definition or modify existing relationship definitions, see the <a href="/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-relationships/">Contributing to Meshery Relationships</a> guide.</p>
</div>
<h2 id="types-of-relationships">
	Types of Relationships
</h2>
<p>Meshery supports different types of relationships to cater to various use cases:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Hierarchical Relationships:</strong> These represent parent-child relationships between components, where one component is a dependency of another. Parent-child relationships show clear lineage, similar to a family tree (child, parent, grandparent, etc.).</li>
<li><strong>Sibling Relationships:</strong> These represent relationships between components that are not directly dependent on each other but may still interact or influence each other&rsquo;s behavior; they describe components that share a common origin but operate independently (siblings, cousins, etc.).</li>
<li><strong>Edge Relationships:</strong> These represent relationships that are visually depicted as edges connecting components in MeshMap. Edge relationships are used to define how components interact with each other, such as network connections, bindings, or permissions. They are also used to identify interdependencies between components.</li>
<li><strong>TagSets Relationships:</strong> These represent relationships between components of same Labels or Annotations key/value pairs. Labels and Annotations are two different types of Tags. Labels are often used to identify components and are visible on the design canvas. Annotations are often used to provide additional information about components.</li>
</ul>
<p>Relationships are categorized into different kinds, types, and subtypes, so that they can be expressive of the specific manner in which one or more components relate to one another. Each type of relationship can be interpreted by Meshery UI (or other <a href="/extensibility/extensions">extensions</a>) and mapped to a specific visual paradigm for the given kind relationship. Let&rsquo;s look at some examples of these visual paradigms; let&rsquo;s explore examples of ways in which relationships are represented in Meshery.</p>
<!-- Broadly, here is a list of the different types of relationships that Meshery supports:

1. Edge
   1. Network
      1. Firewall
      2. Load Balancer
      3. Ingress
   2. Binding
      1. Mount
      2. Permission
2. Hierarchical
   1. Inventory
   2. Parent 
3. TagSets -->
<style>
    figcaption {
        margin: 1rem auto;
    }
</style>
<details open>
    <summary>Example Visual Representations</summary>
    <details close><summary>Kind: Hierarchical</summary>
        <figure>
            <figcaption>subType: Parent | Namespace (Parent) and ConfigMap (child), Role (Child)<a target="_blank" href="https://playground.meshery.io/extension/meshmap?mode=design&design=6370ffcd-13a6-4a65-b426-30f1e63dc381"> (open in playground)</a></figcaption>
        </figure>
        <img alt="Hierarchical - Parent: Namespace to other components" src="/concepts/logical/relationships/images/hierarchical_parent_relationship.svg"/>

<h2 id="the-meaning-of-relationships">
	The Meaning of Relationships
</h2>
<p>Meshery supports a variety of relationships between components. These relationships are categorized into two types: Semantic and Non-Semantic. Relationships are categorized by whether they are meaningful in terms of how Meshery manages entities - a Semantic relationship - or are simply annotations to aid in the comprehension of you as the designer of the relationship - a Non-Semantic relationship.</p>
<h3 id="semantic-relationships">
	Semantic Relationships
</h3>
<p>Semantic relationships are those that are meaningful in the context of the application or infrastructure. For example, a <code>Service</code> in Kubernetes is semantically related to a <code>Deployment</code> or a <code>Pod</code>. These relationships are meaningful and are managed by Meshery.</p>
<h3 id="non-semantic-relationships">
	Non-Semantic Relationships
</h3>
<p>Non-semantic relationships are those that are meaningful to you as a user and your mental representation of your infrastructure and applications, but are not meaningful in terms of how Meshery evaluates the design or manages these relationships and their associated components. Non-semantic relationships are ignored by Meshery&rsquo;s lifecycle management engine. For example, a <code>Rectangle</code> shape that encloses other components (has a parent relationship with other child components) is not semantically meaningful to the way in which Meshery manages these resources. While the <code>Rectangle</code> shape might have a parent-child relationship with any number of Meshery-managed components, such a relationship does not implicate any management that Meshery might perform; they are not managed by Meshery.</p>
<!-- @iArchitSharma, help, if you would please.

_[TODO: a visual example is needed here]_ -->
<h4 id="identifying-non-semantic-relationships">
	Identifying Non-Semantic Relationships
</h4>
<p>The <code>isAnnotation</code> attribute of a Relationship or Component determines whether the given Relationship or Component represents a management concern for Meshery; whether the given Relationship or Component is semantically meaningful, and whose lifecycle is managed by Meshery.</p>
<h2 id="core-concepts-of-relationships">
	Core Concepts of Relationships
</h2>
<ul>
<li>Kinds</li>
<li>Types</li>
<li>Subtypes</li>
<li>Selectors</li>
<li>Selectors Sets</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="kind-type-and-subtype-of-relationships">
	Kind, Type, and Subtype of Relationships
</h2>
<p>The combination of <code>kind</code>, <code>type</code>, and <code>subType</code> uniquely determines the visual paradigm for a given relationship; i.e., relationships with the same <code>kind</code>, <code>type</code>, and <code>subType</code> will share an identical visual representation regardless of the specific components involved in the relationship.</p>

	1. Edge - Network

<ul>
<li>Example 1) Service &ndash;&gt; Deployment</li>
<li>Example 2) IngressController &ndash;&gt; Ingress &ndash;&gt; Service</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="5-edge---reference">
	5. Edge - Reference
</h3>
<p>Logical or declarative links between components where one component refers to another by name, identifier, type, or scope.</p>
<ul>
<li>Example 1) Pod &ndash;&gt; ConfigMap (via envFrom)</li>
<li>Example 2) Pod &ndash;&gt; Secret (via volumes)</li>
</ul>
<details close><summary>Visual Representation of Edge-Reference Relationship</summary>
        <br>
        <p>The <strong>Edge-Reference</strong> relationship type represents a <strong>logical or declarative link</strong> between two components, where one component <strong>refers to another by name, identifier, type, or scope</strong>. This relationship allows components to dynamically locate, associate with, or depend on other components without being tightly coupled to them. It forms the basis for indirect communication, configuration reuse, ownership tracking, and dependency resolution in distributed systems.</p>
        <p>This type of relationship does <strong>not directly provide communication, access, or permission</strong>, but <strong>enables such interactions by declaring intent or pointing to another component</strong>.</p>
